method: Headlines from the source feed, read by Claude: summary and four beats in Blue Street's own words from each article's headline and public text; impact = which way the headline pushes each market (dir bullish/bearish/mixed, strength 1 mild, 2 clear, 3 strong). Evidence, not a call.

USD.text: The dollar closed at a three-week low near 101.7 on its index as Treasury yields eased and housing data was weak. A December Fed hike is still expected, which keeps a floor under it.

EUR.text: The euro rose toward 1.126 as oil eased on Tuesday, but debt worries kept it near a three-month low on the franc, and a report that Putin ordered sabotage across NATO adds a security worry. France's budget vote is Oct 27.

GBP.text: Sterling sits near five-week highs around 1.34 after a strong jobs report, with a November BoE hike almost fully priced. Wednesday's inflation figure, expected to rise to 3.4%, can confirm that or knock it back.

JPY.text: Japan's finance minister said she sees no gap with the BoJ, and most economists now expect a hike to 1.50% in December, which helps the yen over time. But oil back near $110 and a wider-than-expected trade deficit keep weighing on it now.

CHF.text: Europe's debt worries lifted the franc to a three-month high on the euro, near where the SNB has warned it may act. A real US-Iran deal would ease the need for shelter.

CAD.text: Bets on an Oct 28 BoC hike have more than doubled and big Canadian banks now expect one, lifting the loonie. Oil's afternoon drop on US-Iran talk is the risk if it holds.

AUD.text: The Aussie holds above 70 US cents after RBA Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser said inflation will likely beat the bank's forecast, lifting the odds of a November 3 hike. China setting its yuan weaker than expected is a small drag.

NZD.text: The kiwi edged up as world dairy prices had their best auction since February, and about 80% odds of an Oct 28 RBNZ hike are priced. This week's Q3 inflation figure decides whether that holds.

XAU.text: Gold fell for a fourth day, to about $4,120, as costlier oil revived bets on a December Fed hike. A lasting fall in US yields would ease that weight.

OIL.text: Brent crude rose back toward $110 after a supertanker hit a mine south of the shut Strait of Hormuz and ship attacks spread to the Gulf of Oman, the route used to get around it. US-Iran mediation goes on, but nothing is agreed.

items.headline: Gold falls for a fourth session as oil revives rate-hike bets
items.story_title: Gold: oil, yields and the Fed
items.summary: Gold slipped to around $4,117–4,120 an ounce, a fourth straight daily fall, as higher oil revived bets that the Federal Reserve raises rates in December.

beats.was: Gold climbed to records through the year, but the Gulf war's oil shock has pushed up inflation and with it the chance of higher US interest rates, which hurt a metal that pays no interest.
beats.happened: Oil rose after a diplomat played down talk of an imminent US-Iran deal, and gold edged down about 0.1–0.2%. The Fed is expected to hold next week, with a December hike seen as possible.
beats.means: For now gold is trading more on US rate expectations than as a war shelter.
beats.fx: Costlier oil → higher US inflation → more chance of a Fed hike → less appeal for gold. The lens: a real fall in US yields would turn this.

impact.why: Rate-hike bets keep weighing on a metal that pays no interest.

items.watch: Next week's Fed meeting and any shift in December hike odds; a lasting drop in oil.

items.headline: UK CPI is expected to confirm the inflationary impact of high energy prices
items.story_title: BoE: the November decision
items.summary: UK inflation for September, due at 06:00 GMT Wednesday, is expected to rise to 3.4% from 3.1%, with the core rate up to 2.8%, as costly energy feeds into prices.

beats.was: The Bank of England has not raised rates this year, but a strong jobs report and warnings on sticky pay have markets almost fully expecting a quarter-point hike at its November meeting.
beats.happened: Forecasters expect headline inflation of 3.4% over the year to September, from 3.1% in August, and 0.3% on the month. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, is seen at 2.8% from 2.6%.
beats.means: A figure in line or higher would back the November hike; a soft one would raise doubts, since the hike is already mostly priced.
beats.fx: Hot print → hike confirmed → firmer pound; soft print → hike in doubt → pound gives back its recent gains. The lens: core and services prices, not just the headline.

impact.why: A preview: the pound's direction depends on whether the figure beats or misses.

items.watch: The 06:00 GMT release, especially core and services inflation.

items.headline: US intel says Putin ordered NATO sabotage drive, Leipzig drone attack an opening shot
items.story_title: Russia–NATO: sabotage and grey-zone attacks
items.summary: The Wall Street Journal reports US intelligence concluded Russian President Vladimir Putin personally ordered a sabotage campaign against NATO countries, including an August drone attack on a German airport.

beats.was: Since August Europe has seen a string of suspected Russian attacks short of war: arson in Estonia and Poland, damage to Starlink stations and drone hits on ships in the Black Sea. Germany blamed Russia in September for a failed drone strike on a military-aid plane at Leipzig-Halle airport.
beats.happened: Citing European officials, the Journal says US intelligence found the campaign was ordered by Putin and run by a Russian military-intelligence unit. Aides to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said heavy casualties at Leipzig would have led Germany to weigh NATO's mutual-defence clause. Russia denies any role.
beats.means: It puts a name on attacks already known rather than reporting a new one, but it raises the chance of a tougher European response.
beats.fx: More security risk on Europe's doorstep → small weight on the euro and a small pull toward the franc as shelter. Little effect unless governments act. The lens: any new sanctions or a hit to Russian fuel supply?

impact.why: Raises the risk of a sharper Russia–NATO standoff near the euro area.
Mild extra demand for a safe place to park money.

items.watch: A formal European response or new sanctions; any disruption to Russian diesel exports.

items.headline: PBOC sets USD/CNY mid-point today at 6.7192 (vs. estimate at 6.6779)
items.story_title: China: Beijing slows the yuan's climb
items.summary: China's central bank set the yuan's daily reference rate about 0.6% weaker than analysts expected, another sign Beijing wants to slow the currency's rise.

beats.was: Each morning the People's Bank of China sets a midpoint for the yuan, which can trade 2% either side of it. Since late last year it has often set it weaker than models predict, to slow a yuan that has been near its strongest in over three years.
beats.happened: The bank set the rate at 6.7192 per dollar, against a Reuters estimate of 6.6779, a gap of about 0.6%. It gave no reason, which is normal.
beats.means: Beijing is still leaning against a fast-rising yuan, likely to protect exporters. It is a familiar move, not a new policy.
beats.fx: A softer yuan on purpose → China's trade partners get a little less lift from it → slight weight on the Aussie and kiwi, which trade as China proxies. The lens: does the gap keep widening?

impact.why: A held-back yuan takes a little shine off China-linked currencies.
Same China link, smaller effect.

items.watch: Whether the daily gap to estimates grows larger; China's next round of growth support.

items.headline: Japan's Katayama sees no gap with BOJ, says wage-driven inflation is near
items.story_title: BoJ: when the next hike comes
items.summary: Japan's Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama told parliament the government and the Bank of Japan see things the same way, and that pay-driven inflation is close, a condition the BoJ wants before raising rates again.

beats.was: Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's government plans a consumption tax cut and cash handouts, and investors have worried it could clash with the Bank of Japan's rate rises; in September two board members picked by the government voted against the hike to 1.25%.
beats.happened: Katayama said today's price rises come mostly from import costs, but the economy is close to inflation driven by rising wages. Asked about a clash with the BoJ, she said the two sides talk and she sees no gap. She did not openly back more hikes.
beats.means: It lowers the odds that the government stands in the way of the next hike, which most economists expect in December.
beats.fx: Less political pushback → a December BoJ hike looks safer → mild support for the yen. The lens: do the government's picks on the board keep dissenting?

impact.why: Eases fears that the government blocks further rate rises.

items.watch: Friday's Japan inflation figures and the BoJ's Oct 29–30 meeting, including how its board votes.

items.headline: Oil rises on Middle East supply and shipping concerns
items.story_title: Hormuz: mines, tanker hits and blockade threats
items.summary: Brent crude climbed back toward $110 in Asian trading after Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a supertanker caught fire on a mine south of the Strait of Hormuz, and analysts said ship attacks now reach the Gulf of Oman.

beats.was: The Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, has been shut since the US-Iran war began this month, and Gulf exporters have leaned on loading points outside it, such as the Gulf of Oman, to keep crude moving.
beats.happened: Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said a supertanker hit a sea mine and caught fire south of the strait. LSEG analysts said attacks have spread as far as the Gulf of Oman; the ship tracker Kpler counts at least 18 attacks on vessels in two weeks. Yemen's Houthi rebels also claimed strikes on Saudi oil sites at Yanbu and Shaybah. Brent rose about 0.8% to $109.64.
beats.means: The workaround routes that kept Middle East oil flowing are now in range too, so a quick return to normal supply looks less likely even while mediation talks go on.
beats.fx: Attacks outside the strait → less oil getting out → higher crude → support for oil exporters like Canada, and a bigger import bill for Japan and Europe. The lens: do loadings in the Gulf of Oman actually slow?

impact.why: Attacks are reaching the routes used to bypass the shut strait.
Higher crude lifts Canada's export income.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so a costlier barrel weighs on the yen.

items.watch: Whether tanker loadings off Oman drop, and any reply to Iran's mediation offer; Wednesday's US crude stock report.

items.headline: Japan exports rise 16.7% for 13th straight month on AI chip demand, trade gap narrows
items.story_title: Japan: exports, the oil bill and the yen
items.summary: Japan's exports grew 16.7% from a year earlier in September, a 13th straight rise but well short of the 20% expected, so the trade deficit came in wider than forecast at about ¥537 billion.

beats.was: Japan's exports have been lifted all year by demand for chips and AI equipment, while costly oil, pushed up by the Gulf war, has swollen the import bill and kept the country in trade deficit.
beats.happened: Japan's Ministry of Finance said September exports rose 16.7% from a year earlier, against about 20% expected and 19.3% in August. Imports rose 18.9%, slower than August's 28%. The deficit was about ¥537 billion, against ¥181 billion expected but half of August's roughly ¥1.1 trillion.
beats.means: Overseas demand for Japanese goods is still solid but cooling, and the energy bill remains the drag. A smaller gap than August helps a little, but the miss gives the Bank of Japan, which meets Oct 29–30, no new reason to hurry a rate rise.
beats.fx: Exports slower than hoped, oil still costly → more yen sold to pay for imports than expected → mild pressure on the yen. The lens: is the oil bill shrinking, or just pausing?

impact.why: Exports missed and the deficit beat forecasts, though it halved from August.

items.watch: The Bank of Japan's Oct 29–30 meeting and its new forecasts; a lasting drop in oil would shrink the import bill.

items.headline: Australian central banker says policy working, but inflation outlook worse
items.story_title: RBA: the November 3 decision
items.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia's deputy governor, Andrew Hauser, said inflation now looks set to run above the bank's own forecast, raising the odds of another rate rise on November 3. The Aussie pushed above 70 US cents.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of Australia has already raised its cash rate four times this year, to 4.60%, to fight inflation lifted partly by the Gulf war's hit to oil. It next decides on November 3.
beats.happened: Speaking at a Citi conference in Sydney, Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser said higher rates are slowing the economy, but the inflation outlook has got clearly worse, partly because of high oil prices. Markets raised the chance of a November hike to 4.85% to about 40%, from 30% at the start of the week, and AUD/USD rose to about 0.701, a two-week high.
beats.means: A senior official saying inflation will beat the bank's forecast keeps a fifth hike on the table, even with unemployment at a five-year high of 4.7% and house prices falling. Next week's third-quarter inflation figure, seen near 4%, is the deciding number.
beats.fx: Inflation running hotter than the RBA expected → more chance of a rate rise → higher returns on Australian dollars → Aussie up. The lens: does next week's inflation figure back him up?

impact.why: Hike odds for Nov 3 rose to about 40% and the Aussie broke above 0.70.

items.watch: Australia's third-quarter inflation figure next week; a soft print, or weaker jobs and housing, would cool hike bets.

items.headline: BOJ seen lifting rates to 1.50% in December as 69% of economists expect a Q4 hike
items.story_title: BoJ: when the next hike comes
items.summary: A Reuters poll of 78 economists found 69% now expect the Bank of Japan to raise rates to 1.50% by year-end, almost double September's share, with December the favourite month.

beats.was: The Bank of Japan raised its rate in June and again in September, to 1.25%, but the yen has stayed close to its weakest level of the year because US rates are far higher.
beats.happened: In the poll, taken Oct 13–19, 54 of 78 economists expect a hike to 1.50% this quarter, up from 36% a month ago. About 80% of those naming a month picked December; only 2% expect a move at the meeting ending Oct 30. Half now see rates reaching 2% or more.
beats.means: Forecasters see the BoJ moving faster than they thought a month ago, but not next week.
beats.fx: More hikes expected → Japan's rate gap with the US narrows over time → slow support for the yen. The lens: does the BoJ hint at December when it meets Oct 30?

impact.why: Economists now expect a quicker climb in Japan's rates.

items.watch: The BoJ's Oct 29–30 statement and new forecasts; most in the poll warned that more board dissent could weigh on the yen.

items.headline: Milk powder gains fuel GDT price surge
items.story_title: NZ dairy prices
items.summary: World dairy prices rose 2.5% at Tuesday's Global Dairy Trade auction, the most since February, led by the milk powders New Zealand sells most.

beats.was: The Global Dairy Trade auction runs twice a month and sets prices for New Zealand's biggest export, so it feeds farm incomes and the kiwi.
beats.happened: The overall index rose 2.5%. Whole milk powder gained 4.4% and skim milk powder 3.4%, while butter and milk fat slipped.
beats.means: Milk powder is what most decides NZ farmers' milk price, so forecasts for this season's payout may rise. Fonterra could update its forecast before its Nov 12 shareholder meeting.
beats.fx: Higher dairy prices → more export income for New Zealand → more demand for kiwi. The lens: does the gain hold at the next auction in early November?

impact.why: Best auction since February, led by the main export product.

items.watch: Fonterra's milk price forecast and NZ third-quarter inflation figures this week.

items.headline: Forex Today: UK inflation comes to the fore
items.story_title: BoE: the November decision
items.summary: A calmer risk mood left the dollar at a three-week low and the pound above 1.34 going into Wednesday's UK inflation report, which decides how sure a November BoE hike really is.

beats.was: A wrap of Tuesday's moves and a look at what comes next, led by UK consumer prices on Wednesday.
beats.happened: The dollar index briefly touched about 101.5, its lowest in three weeks. The pound reached five-week highs just over 1.34, the Aussie neared 0.70, and gold slipped toward $4,100 even with a softer dollar.
beats.means: Markets already expect the BoE to hike in November. A firm inflation print would confirm that; a soft one is the main way the pound's run could stall.
beats.fx: Hot UK prices → hike locked in, maybe more → higher UK yields → pound supported. The lens: does inflation back up the jobs data?

impact.why: At five-week highs ahead of CPI, which can confirm or puncture the hike case.
Eased toward $4,100 despite a weaker dollar and lower yields.

items.watch: Wednesday's UK CPI; any official word on the US-Iran plan.

items.headline: BoE's Greene warns stalled wage disinflation raises inflation risks
items.story_title: BoE: the November decision
items.summary: Bank of England rate-setter Megan Greene said UK pay growth has stopped cooling at a level too high for 2% inflation, and the Bank should act early against it.

beats.was: Megan Greene sits on the Bank of England's nine-member rate committee and has long been one of its firmest voices for keeping rates high.
beats.happened: In a speech a day before UK inflation figures, she said pay growth has stalled above what fits a 2% inflation target and the risk of higher prices feeding into wages is bigger than the Bank thought.
beats.means: It backs the case for a hike at the Nov 5 meeting, which markets already price almost fully. It's one known hawk repeating her view, so it adds weight rather than news.
beats.fx: Sticky pay → more pressure to hike → UK yields stay high → support for the pound. The lens: do other committee members say the same?

impact.why: A rate-setter backing early action; a Nov 5 hike was already near fully priced.

items.watch: Wednesday's UK consumer prices: a soft figure would weaken her case.

items.headline: US Treasury yields retreat as Iran deal hopes pull WTI lower
items.story_title: US–Iran: a mediated plan to restart talks
items.summary: Long-term US yields edged down on deal hopes while two-year yields held flat, so markets still expect the Fed to hike in December.

beats.was: US government bond yields, which set how much dollar assets pay.
beats.happened: The 10-year yield slipped about 2bp to near 5.12% and the 2-year held near 4.79%. WTI eased below $98 and the dollar index lost about 0.3%.
beats.means: The dip is small and only at the long end. Short-term yields, which track the Fed, didn't move, so the case for a December hike is intact.
beats.fx: Small dip in long yields → slight loss of dollar support; flat 2-year → Fed outlook unchanged. The lens: does the 2-year start to fall too?

impact.why: Long yields eased, but Fed pricing didn't budge.
Lower yields ease the main weight on gold.

items.watch: Thursday's jobless claims and Friday's flash PMIs; the Fed meets Oct 27-28.

items.headline: Dollar Index drops on Iran deal report, steadies on denial
items.story_title: US–Iran: a mediated plan to restart talks
items.summary: The dollar hit its lowest since Oct 1 on the US-Iran report, then won some back after a diplomat said a deal wasn't close.

beats.was: The dollar's reaction to reports that both sides had backed a Qatar-Pakistan plan.
beats.happened: The dollar index fell to just above 101.5, then bounced near 101.7 on the denial. Weak housing data added to the softness.
beats.means: The dollar has given back about a third of its rise since early September. Economists still all expect a Fed hike in December, which keeps a floor under it.
beats.fx: Peace hopes → cheaper oil → lower yields and less haven demand → dollar softer. The lens: is the US-Iran plan real?

impact.why: Three-week low on the report, partly undone by the denial.
Rose as oil fell, the mirror of the dollar's drop.

items.watch: Any official confirmation; Thursday's jobless claims and Friday's flash PMIs.

items.headline: British Pound surges to 1.3400 as UK jobs beat, Iran deal hopes grow
items.story_title: BoE: the November decision
items.summary: The pound gained about 0.7% to near 1.34 as a strong jobs report met a softer dollar on US-Iran hopes.

beats.was: Sterling's move after the UK jobs report and the US-Iran reports.
beats.happened: The UK added about 102,000 jobs in three months, well above forecasts, and unemployment fell. Markets now see about a 93% chance of a November BoE hike.
beats.means: Two forces lined up at once: a firmer case for UK rates and a weaker dollar. The pound sits right under a cluster of resistance near 1.341.
beats.fx: Strong jobs → BoE hike nearly certain → higher UK yields → pound up; softer dollar adds to it. The lens: does CPI confirm?

impact.why: Up about 0.7% to five-week highs, building on the jobs beat.
Softer on US-Iran hopes and weak housing data.

items.watch: Wednesday's UK CPI; a denial of the US-Iran plan would help the dollar back.

items.headline: US Iran breakthrough this week? $6 billion frozen funds, secret nuclear inspection in new peace proposal
items.story_title: US–Iran: a mediated plan to restart talks
items.summary: What the reported plan contains: Iran would get the interest, not the principal, on $6 billion frozen in Qatar, and would allow a quiet UN nuclear inspection. Neither government has confirmed it.

beats.was: The terms of the Qatar-Pakistan proposal, carried to Tehran by Pakistan's army chief.
beats.happened: A Qatari-owned paper, citing unnamed sources, said the US agreed and Iran responded well. Iranian sources later said reports of a near deal were wrong, while saying talks go on.
beats.means: It is a small first step on money and inspections, not a peace deal. It matters because it would reopen talks after weeks of escalation.
beats.fx: Real talks → lower odds of Gulf supply cuts → less demand for safe havens and less oil premium. The lens: do both sides confirm?

impact.why: An unconfirmed opening for talks, already partly denied.
Talks hope eases the need for shelter.

items.watch: Official word from Washington or Tehran; a new tanker or Saudi attack would undercut it.

items.headline: WTI Oil slides as US-Iran compromise plan eases Middle East risks
items.story_title: US–Iran: a mediated plan to restart talks
items.summary: US crude gave back its surge, falling to about $95.70 after briefly topping $100, on a report that Washington and Tehran had tentatively backed a mediated plan. Nothing is officially confirmed.

beats.was: A report of a Pakistan- and Qatar-brokered plan to get the US and Iran talking again.
beats.happened: Israeli TV said the US approved it and Iran gave early consent. WTI swung from above $100 to near $95.70, down about 2.4% on the day.
beats.means: Oil had been pricing a long squeeze on Gulf supply. Any path to talks shrinks that war premium fast, even before anything is signed.
beats.fx: Talks hope → less war premium in oil → lower inflation fears → softer yields → oil sellers' currencies lose a tailwind. The lens: is the plan confirmed, or just a report?

impact.why: Talk of a deal knocked out much of the day's surge.
Cheaper oil trims the loonie's main support.
Lower oil pulls US yields and hike bets back.

items.watch: An official denial or a new attack on ships would rebuild the premium; a confirmed meeting would deepen the drop.

items.headline: Euro climbs as Oil prices tumble on US-Iran negotiation hopes
items.story_title: US–Iran: a mediated plan to restart talks
items.summary: The dollar index slipped to its lowest since Oct 1 as oil and US 10-year yields fell on US-Iran talks hope. EUR/USD rose to about 1.125.

beats.was: The euro-dollar rate during the US session.
beats.happened: EUR/USD rose about 0.35% to near 1.125. The dollar index fell to about 101.55, off last week's 18-month high near 103, and the US 10-year yield dropped about 6 basis points to around 5.08%.
beats.means: The dollar's recent strength rode on oil-driven yields. When oil eases, that support fades, and Europe, a big oil importer, gets some relief.
beats.fx: Oil down → US yields down → dollar's yield edge narrows → dollar slips, euro gains. The lens: does oil keep falling?

impact.why: Dollar index fell to a near three-week low as yields dropped.
Cheaper oil eases Europe's import bill and lifts the euro.

items.watch: Houthi strikes and Hormuz ship attacks are still live; a fresh hit would send oil and the dollar back up.

items.headline: Pakistan army chief in Tehran: Can diplomacy prevent new US-Iran fighting?
items.story_title: US-Iran: mediation and the oil swing
items.summary: Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir flew to Tehran to keep US-Iran talks alive, while US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met Israel's leader amid talk of new strikes.

beats.was: Pakistan brokered the April 8 US-Iran ceasefire. A June deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and lift the US naval blockade lapsed in August, and the strait is still shut.
beats.happened: Field Marshal Asim Munir arrived in Tehran on his fifth visit since the ceasefire. Talks are indirect, with Qatar passing proposals. US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, reportedly about resuming major strikes.
beats.means: Diplomacy is busy but nothing is agreed, and the threat of new fighting hasn't gone. President Trump has said the US won't strike before the Nov 3 midterms.
beats.fx: Talks progress → Hormuz reopening hopes → lower oil → relief for oil importers (euro, yen); talks fail → new fighting → oil up, safe havens up. The lens: does mediation turn into a signed step?

impact.why: Mediation keeps a reopening possible, but strike talk keeps supply risk alive.
Shelter demand rises or falls with the chance of renewed fighting.

items.watch: Any signed step on Hormuz or the blockade; signs the US or Israel is preparing new strikes.

items.headline: Physical Gold Slips To $4,124 As Oil-Driven Yields Revive Fed Hike Bets; Silver Firms
items.story_title: Gold: oil, yields and the Fed
items.summary: Gold fell for a third day to about $4,124 as oil pushed US yields toward 5.14% and markets leaned harder into a December Fed hike.

beats.was: The daily gold price and what moved it.
beats.happened: Spot gold was down about 0.4% to near $4,124, a third straight loss, while silver edged up.
beats.means: Higher oil means stickier inflation, so the Fed may have to hike again. That lifts yields, and gold pays no interest, so holding it gets costlier.
beats.fx: Dearer oil → Fed hike odds up → higher US yields → cash and bonds pay more than gold → gold slips. The lens: where are US yields heading?

impact.why: Third daily loss as yields rise on oil.
December hike bets firming gives the dollar a yield edge.

items.watch: A pullback in oil or yields would lift gold; a confirmed supply loss could revive haven buying.

items.headline: Swiss Franc Recovery Tests SNB Tolerance Against Euro
items.story_title: Franc: haven demand vs the SNB
items.summary: The franc climbed to a three-month high against the euro on fears of a European debt crisis, nearing levels where the SNB has threatened to step in.

beats.was: The franc's comeback against the euro after months of weakness.
beats.happened: EUR/CHF fell to a three-month low as money sought shelter from Europe's debt worries and Switzerland's sounder public finances.
beats.means: The franc is near the zone where the SNB warned it could sell francs. That threat caps gains unless the euro area's problems get worse.
beats.fx: European debt fears → money into a safe, low-debt neighbour → franc up, until the SNB pushes back. The lens: does France's budget fight get worse?

impact.why: Haven demand lifted it, but the SNB's line is close.
Debt worries pushed it to a three-month low on the franc.

items.watch: Any SNB intervention or warning; France's Oct 27 budget vote.

items.headline: Yen jumps after JGB auction draws big demand, euro finds relief
items.story_title: Japan: tax cuts and the bond bill
items.summary: Buyers swamped Japan's 20-year bond sale with record demand, pulling yields down and giving the yen its first gain in three days.

beats.was: Japan sold 20-year government bonds, a test of whether investors will fund its growing borrowing.
beats.happened: Bids came in at 5.84 times the amount on offer, the most since these bonds began in 1987, against 4.01 last month. The 20-year yield fell 6bp to 3.71% and the yen rose to about 158.1 per dollar.
beats.means: Fears that Japan's tax cuts would scare off bond buyers eased for now, and some investors see Japanese bonds as a calmer place than France. It eases one source of yen weakness, but the gap with US rates is still wide.
beats.fx: Strong bond demand → less fear over Japan's debt → steadier yields and money staying home → yen firmer. The lens: is Japan's fiscal risk fading or just paused?

impact.why: Record auction demand eased debt fears and snapped a two-day slide.
Edged up to about 1.123 as pressure from France eased overnight.

items.watch: Friday's Japan CPI and any sign the auction demand doesn't repeat; a US yield jump would undo the gain.

items.headline: Euro rebounds as French protests ease, dollar slips
items.story_title: France: unrest, budget vote and the euro
items.summary: The euro bounced as French protests calmed under curfews, but France's budget vote is still due today and some banks expect more euro weakness.

beats.was: A check on the euro after two days of nationwide unrest in France, with lawmakers voting on the 2027 budget's revenue side.
beats.happened: The euro rose 0.2% to about 1.123, off last week's low near 1.111. The dollar index slipped to about 101.75, near the bottom of its October range. The Canadian dollar firmed after Alberta voted to stay in Canada.
beats.means: Calmer streets bought the euro a breather, not a fix: worries about France's finances have weighed since September and the budget is still unresolved. Brent above $110 is a cushion for the dollar.
beats.fx: Less unrest → less fear over French debt → euro steadies. The lens: does the budget pass without new stress in French bonds?

impact.why: Bounced as protests eased, but the budget risk and Friday's Moody's review remain.
Near a one-month high after Alberta voted to remain in Canada, removing a tail risk.
Dollar index slipped as pressure on the euro eased.

items.watch: The French budget vote and the gap between French and German yields; Moody's review of France on Friday.

items.headline: German producer prices climb 6.7% in September, above forecasts
items.story_title: Euro area: price pressure and the ECB
items.summary: German factory-gate prices rose faster than expected, a sign that costs are still feeding through to what shoppers will pay.

beats.was: Producer prices: what German firms charge for goods as they leave the factory, an early read on future consumer inflation.
beats.happened: They were up 6.7% from a year earlier, against forecasts near 6.2%.
beats.means: With the ECB's target at 2%, pipeline prices this hot keep pressure on it to lean hawkish, though markets already treat December, not October, as the live meeting.
beats.fx: Hotter costs → more pressure on the ECB → higher euro yields → some support for the euro. The lens: do these costs reach shop prices?

impact.why: A hot cost print adds to the case for a December ECB hike, but France still dominates.

items.watch: Euro-area flash PMIs and the October ECB meeting on Oct 29 for how much weight the bank puts on this.

items.headline: Brent crude hovers near $110 on Middle East tensions
items.story_title: Saudi–Houthi fighting and the Gulf supply risk
items.summary: Brent edged up toward $110 after Houthi claims of strikes on a Saudi oil field and airports, plus fresh hints from Israel and the US of more action against Iran.

beats.was: Oil's early Tuesday move, set by war risk around Saudi Arabia and Iran.
beats.happened: Brent rose about 0.3% to near $109.9 and WTI held near $98.6. The Houthis said they hit Saudi Arabia's Shaybah oil field and airports in Riyadh and Abha, though there's no confirmation that output was affected.
beats.means: The claims are unconfirmed, so this is risk being priced rather than barrels lost. But talk of more action against Iran keeps the floor under oil.
beats.fx: Higher war risk → pricier oil → better terms of trade for oil sellers, worse for importers → Canadian dollar helped, yen hurt. The lens: are Saudi barrels actually being lost?

impact.why: Unconfirmed strike claims on Saudi oil sites and Iran threats keep the risk premium.
An oil exporter gains when crude holds near its highs.
Japan imports its oil, so a high price widens its import bill.

items.watch: Any confirmation of damage at Shaybah, or US–Iran mediation progress, which would let the premium fade.

items.headline: US pending home sales tumble to record low in September
items.story_title: US housing: frozen by 7%+ mortgages
items.summary: Signed home-sale contracts fell 7.3% in September to the lowest level on record, far worse than the small dip expected. Mortgage rates above 7% are freezing buyers.

beats.was: Pending home sales count contracts signed on existing homes, an early read on sales a month or two ahead.
beats.happened: Contracts fell 7.3% in a month, against a 0.5% dip forecast, and are down about 11% on a year ago. Every region fell.
beats.means: War-driven inflation pushed Treasury yields up, and 30-year mortgages near 7.4% have priced many buyers out. Housing is where high rates bite first, so the US economy is starting to feel the squeeze.
beats.fx: Housing slumps → growth cools → less room for the Fed to keep hiking → softer yield support → dollar loses a little shine. The lens: does the weakness spread past housing?

impact.why: A record-low print, far below forecast, shows high rates starting to hurt growth.

items.watch: If mortgage rates ease or other data hold firm, this stays a housing story rather than a growth scare.

items.headline: US homebuilding slows in September as construction activity, permits decline
items.story_title: US housing: frozen by 7%+ mortgages
items.summary: US housing starts fell 5.2% in September to a four-month low, when a small rise was expected. Permits held up better than feared.

beats.was: Housing starts count new homes builders broke ground on; permits show what is lined up next.
beats.happened: Starts dropped 5.2% to a 1.22 million yearly pace against a forecast rise of about 2%. Permits slipped only 0.2%, less than the drop expected.
beats.means: Builders are pulling back as high borrowing costs thin out buyers. Steady permits say the pipeline hasn't collapsed yet.
beats.fx: Weaker building → slower growth → a little less pressure on the Fed to hike → dollar slightly softer. The lens: is this a dip or a trend?

impact.why: Starts missed badly, though permits softened the blow.

items.watch: October permits: a sharp drop there would confirm builders are retreating.

items.headline: US-Israel-Iran war: Lull nears 'breaking point' — US, Israel weighing new strikes?
items.story_title: Hormuz: mines, tanker hits and blockade threats
items.summary: Reports say the US and Israel are weighing new strikes on Iran as talks stall, while Iran's Guards threaten undersea cables through Hormuz. Much of it is unverified.

beats.was: A daily roundup of the US-Israel-Iran war, now about eight months in with major fighting paused.
beats.happened: Diplomacy has stalled and reports say new US and Israeli strikes are under consideration. Iran's Guards claim the strait is closed; the US says commercial ships still pass.
beats.means: The pause looks fragile. A return to strikes would hit oil supply again and push markets toward safety.
beats.fx: Risk of renewed strikes → higher oil risk premium and safe-haven demand → oil up, franc and yen supported. The lens: do the talks Qatar says are continuing hold?

impact.why: Talk of new strikes adds to the supply risk premium; not confirmed.
A fragile pause keeps haven demand alive.

items.watch: Confirmed strikes would be a real escalation; progress in Qatar-brokered talks would cool it.

items.headline: Middle East War: Attempted strikes on US ships 'unsuccessful', Hegseth visits region
items.story_title: Saudi–Houthi fighting and the Gulf supply risk
items.summary: US crude jumped about 6% toward $110 as the Houthis fired at Riyadh again and the US defence chief made a surprise trip to the region. Iran's attempts to hit US ships near Hormuz reportedly failed.

beats.was: A day of war news around the Gulf: Houthi missiles at Saudi Arabia, Iran's mines in Hormuz, and a surprise visit by the US defence secretary.
beats.happened: A Houthi missile aimed at Riyadh was intercepted and the city's airport stayed shut. US crude rose about 5.7% to roughly $109.60 and Brent about 2% to near $111.70.
beats.means: Oil is pricing more than one route at risk at once: Hormuz and the Saudi coast. A senior US visit suggests next steps are being weighed, so traders keep paying for the risk.
beats.fx: More attacks → more fear for supply → dearer oil → oil sellers like the loonie gain, oil buyers like Japan pay more → yen under pressure. The lens: does any oil actually stop flowing?

impact.why: US crude up about 6% in a day as attacks spread to more targets.
Canada sells oil, so a higher price helps its trade.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so a dearer barrel drains it.
War headlines keep some shelter demand under the franc.

items.watch: Any confirmed halt in Saudi or Hormuz exports would push this higher; a US–Iran deal or a lull in attacks would pull it back.

items.headline: Loonie Rallies as Oil Surge and Weaker Dollar Hit USD/CAD
items.story_title: Bank of Canada: hike talk vs cooling core
items.summary: The loonie rose for a fourth day, with USD/CAD near 1.409, as oil climbed. Middle East crude flows have reportedly fallen to well under half their normal level.

beats.was: A daily read on the Canadian dollar against the US dollar.
beats.happened: USD/CAD slid for a fourth session to around 1.409. Tanker-tracker Kpler puts Middle East crude flows near 8.5 million barrels a day, down from over 20 million.
beats.means: Canada gets paid more for each barrel it sells while Gulf supply is squeezed. RBC still sees the BoC on hold, torn between weak growth and oil-led inflation.
beats.fx: Gulf flows cut → higher oil → more money for Canadian exports → demand for loonies → CAD up. The lens: how long does the oil squeeze last?

impact.why: Fourth day of gains as oil rises; USD/CAD near 1.409.
Reported Gulf crude flows down by more than half.
Softer against the oil currencies to start the week.

items.watch: A drop in oil or a cautious BoC on Oct 28 would take the wind out of the loonie.

items.headline: Canadian Dollar: October hike bets fuel gains against US Dollar - MUFG
items.story_title: BoC: the October 28 decision
items.summary: Markets more than doubled their bets on a Bank of Canada hike next week, and MUFG expects one, which has helped the loonie.

beats.was: A bank's read on why the Canadian dollar is gaining.
beats.happened: About 21bp of BoC hikes are now priced, up from 9bp late last week, and three big Canadian banks now call for an October hike. USD/CAD fell to about 1.407.
beats.means: Rising household inflation expectations push the BoC to act. The risk is weak jobs: Canada lost many jobs in September.
beats.fx: Hike bets rise → higher Canadian yields → money into CAD → loonie up. The lens: does the BoC deliver on Oct 28?

impact.why: Adds to hike bets already building; a repeat of the shift.

items.watch: The BoC decision on Oct 28; weak data before it would cool the bets.

items.headline: Oil parked above $110 a barrel as IEA warns energy markets won't return to normal next year
items.story_title: Hormuz: reopening offer vs ship attacks
items.summary: The IEA's chief said energy markets won't be back to normal in 2027, warning that Hormuz could close again and diesel costs have roughly doubled.

beats.was: A warning from the head of the West's energy watchdog on how long the supply shock lasts.
beats.happened: Fatih Birol said he sees no path to normal markets next year. Brent was above $111 that morning, and IEA members hold about 1.6 billion barrels in reserve if needed.
beats.means: It argues the oil premium is a long-run issue, not a spike. Fuel, not just crude, is where the strain shows, which keeps inflation pressure alive.
beats.fx: Lasting energy strain → higher import bills and inflation → good for oil exporters like CAD, harder on importers like EUR and JPY. The lens: how long does Gulf supply stay at risk?

impact.why: A warning, not new supply loss; prices later fell on the US-Iran report.
A lasting energy bill weighs on a big fuel importer.

items.watch: Further IEA stock releases; any Hormuz reopening or new tanker attack.

items.headline: Oil prices hit five-month high as Houthi escalation worsens supply and inflation fears
items.story_title: Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia
items.summary: Brent climbed past $111, its highest since May, after a string of Houthi attacks on Saudi targets and with Gulf shipping still squeezed.

beats.was: The price of oil, which sets fuel and import bills for every economy and the export income of producers like Canada.
beats.happened: Brent rose about 1.5% to near $111 and US crude to about $101, five-month highs, after the Houthis claimed six attacks on Saudi Arabia on Monday. Emergency stock releases and letting sanctioned tankers sail again have not offset the hit.
beats.means: Supply from the Gulf is still tight and each new attack adds to the risk premium. Dearer fuel feeds inflation, which keeps central banks, the Fed included, leaning toward higher rates.
beats.fx: Oil up → more income for exporters, bigger bills for importers → loonie supported, yen and euro squeezed, and more inflation pressure keeping US yields high. The lens: is Gulf supply getting through or not?

impact.why: Five-month high as attacks keep Gulf supply tight.
Higher crude lifts Canada's export income.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so dearer crude drains the yen.
Oil-driven inflation keeps rate-hike bets and yields up, a drag on gold.

items.watch: A US-Iran deal or proof that Hormuz traffic is recovering would pull the premium out; a confirmed hit to Saudi output would add to it.

items.headline: Explainer-How France's 2027 budget battle could play out
items.story_title: France: unrest, budget vote and the euro
items.summary: France's vote on the tax side of the budget, due today, slipped to Oct 27. The budget minister warned that changes already passed would add about €10 billion to the deficit.

beats.was: The first big vote on France's 2027 budget.
beats.happened: It was pushed back a week because too many amendments are still open. Approved changes would widen the deficit by about €10 billion.
beats.means: Today's test is gone, but the fight runs on. A minority government may have to force the budget through, which could trigger a confidence vote, with Moody's due Friday.
beats.fx: Delay → risk moves to next week → French bonds stay under watch → euro relief stays fragile. The lens: can Paris pass a budget that cuts the deficit?

impact.why: Today's risk is removed, but a wider deficit and a later showdown remain.

items.watch: Moody's on Friday and the Oct 27 vote; a forced passage and confidence motion would raise the stakes.

items.headline: Sterling rises as strong labour market data reinforces rate hike bets
items.story_title: BoE: the November decision
items.summary: UK jobs held up better than feared: unemployment slipped to 4.7% and pay beat forecasts, so a November BoE hike now looks close to a done deal.

beats.was: The UK's monthly jobs report: how many people are out of work and how fast pay is rising.
beats.happened: Unemployment fell to 4.7%, its lowest since mid-2025, and regular pay grew 3.7% a year, faster than expected. Payrolls edged up and vacancies slipped under 700,000.
beats.means: A labour market this firm keeps wage-driven inflation alive, which removes the BoE's main excuse to wait. Markets now price a November 5 hike almost fully.
beats.fx: Firm jobs and pay → BoE more likely to hike → higher UK yields → money into sterling → pound up. The lens: does Wednesday's CPI back it up?

impact.why: Jobs and pay beat, locking in a November hike; up about 0.3% on the dollar and the euro.
Lost ground to sterling, which sits near its best level on the euro since May 2025.

items.watch: Wednesday's UK CPI: a soft print would cool the hike talk; a hot one would add to it.

items.headline: Iran's IRGC says mines halted two tankers crossing Strait of Hormuz
items.story_title: Hormuz: reopening offer vs ship attacks
items.summary: Iran's Guards say their mines set two tankers on fire as they tried to slip through a route Tehran calls illegal. Nobody else has confirmed it yet.

beats.was: A claim from Iran's Revolutionary Guards about ships trying to get around its control of the Strait of Hormuz.
beats.happened: The Guards said two tankers were set ablaze and stopped by mines in the southern part of the strait. The ships weren't named and no shipping firm or government has backed up the claim.
beats.means: Whether or not every detail holds, it's a warning to anyone trying to bypass Iran's terms, which keeps owners and insurers away. That keeps Gulf flows thin and the oil risk premium high.
beats.fx: Riskier Hormuz → fewer ships willing to cross → oil stays dear and investors want shelter → crude and the franc supported, importers like Japan hurt. The lens: are ships still moving through the strait?

impact.why: Unconfirmed, but it deters ships from the bypass routes.
More Gulf danger adds to haven demand.
Threat to the oil supply Japan relies on.

items.watch: Ship names, insurer notices or tracking data would confirm it; quiet traffic numbers would show it's mostly a warning.

items.headline: Canadian Dollar Outperforms on Alberta Vote
items.story_title: Alberta votes to stay in Canada
items.summary: About three in four Alberta voters rejected starting a path to separation, lifting a political risk off the loonie. It gained on the dollar and the euro.

beats.was: A nonbinding Alberta referendum on whether to start a legal process toward leaving Canada. Alberta is the country's main oil province.
beats.happened: Unofficial results show about 76% voted to stay, a clear margin. USD/CAD slid to about 1.4056, down roughly 1.6% from last week's high.
beats.means: A split would have put Canada's oil income in doubt. A decisive no removes that discount and leaves the loonie trading on oil and the Bank of Canada again.
beats.fx: Separation risk off the table → less reason to hold back from Canadian assets → loonie up. The lens: with politics settled, how hawkish is the BoC on Oct 28?

impact.why: A decisive vote to stay removed a risk premium; up about 0.4% on the dollar and euro.

items.watch: The official tally on Oct 29; a much narrower count would revive the doubt.

items.headline: Germany ZEW Survey - Economic Sentiment deteriorates significantly to 28.1 in October
items.story_title: Euro area: growth under the oil and France hit
items.summary: German investors turned gloomier about the next six months than expected, even as they said today's conditions are less bad.

beats.was: The ZEW survey asks financial experts how they see Germany's economy now and six months out.
beats.happened: The outlook gauge fell to 28.1 from 34.7, below the 32 expected; the euro-area reading slid to 18.5. The current-conditions gauge improved to -35.9 from -47.1, better than forecast.
beats.means: Things look a little less bad today, but costly energy, higher bond yields and France's troubles are dimming the outlook. That's weaker footing for the euro area while the ECB fights oil-driven inflation.
beats.fx: Gloomier outlook → softer growth ahead → less room for the ECB to keep tightening → mild weight on the euro. The euro shrugged it off this time. The lens: is Europe's growth bending under the oil shock?

impact.why: Outlook missed forecasts; the euro dipped then recovered near 1.121.

items.watch: Friday's flash PMIs: if they also slide, the growth worry becomes harder for the euro to ignore.

items.headline: BOJ reportedly may upgrade inflation forecast, hold rates steady at next week's meeting
items.story_title: BoJ: when the next hike comes
items.summary: People close to the Bank of Japan say it will likely hold at 1.25% on Oct 30 but nudge up its inflation forecast as oil feeds into prices.

beats.was: A Reuters report, from four sources, on what the Bank of Japan plans for its Oct 30 meeting.
beats.happened: Rates are expected to stay at 1.25% after September's hike, with a slightly higher inflation forecast for fiscal 2027. Markets see almost no move next week and roughly 73% odds of a December hike.
beats.means: A higher forecast is the groundwork for another hike, but not yet. Policymakers reportedly see no broad wage-price spiral, so they can wait.
beats.fx: Hold now → US rates stay far above Japan's → yen stays under pressure; higher forecast → December hike more likely → some support later. The yen barely reacted. The lens: how fast will the BoJ close the gap?

impact.why: No move next week, but a firmer forecast keeps December alive.

items.watch: Friday's Japan CPI; a hot print would lift December odds, a soft one would push the yen back toward its lows.

items.headline: Bank of Canada hike bets grow among economists, traders
items.story_title: Bank of Canada: hike talk vs cooling core
items.summary: Three big Canadian banks switched on Monday to expecting a Bank of Canada hike on Oct 28, and swaps moved to price close to a nine-in-ten chance, even though CPI came in a touch soft.

beats.was: Going into Monday, the Oct 28 meeting looked like a close call between a hold and a first hike to 2.50%.
beats.happened: CPI rose 3.1% a year, a bit under forecast, but the Bank's own surveys showed consumers' long-run inflation expectations at their highest since the post-COVID price spike, and about half of firms plan to pass on higher oil and tariff costs. BMO, RBC and Desjardins flipped to a hike call; swaps priced about 87% odds by mid-afternoon, up from roughly 70% in the morning.
beats.means: Central banks fear expectations more than one month's print: if people expect higher prices, they ask for higher wages and firms raise prices, which keeps inflation going. That outweighed the soft CPI.
beats.fx: Expectations drifting up → BoC more likely to hike now → higher Canadian yields → more pull for the loonie. The lens: does the Bank act on expectations, or wait for prices to prove it?

impact.why: Major banks and swaps moved firmly toward an October hike.

items.watch: A Bloomberg survey consensus still points to a hold; any BoC signal before the Oct 28 quiet period, or a sharp oil drop, could swing the odds back.
